name: Narthanavallabeswarar Temple, Koodalaiyathur
deity: Shiva as Narthanavallabeswarar (Nerikkattunayakar), with the goddess Gnana Shakti (also worshipped as Para Shakti, Purikuzhalaambikai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century); medieval structural temple with later additions
summary: Narthanavallabeswarar is the Tirukkoodalaiyatrur of Sundarar's hymn, set where the Vellaru and Manimutharu rivers meet and honoured as the Dakshina Prayagai, the southern confluence, and remembered as the Lord who danced before Brahma.

sections.history: Koodalaiyathur, the Tirukkoodalaiyatrur of the Tevaram, takes its name from its setting: koodal means a joining, and the village stands where the Vellaru and Manimutharu rivers meet. For this reason it is also revered as the Dakshina Prayagai, the southern counterpart of the great confluence of the north. The temple is praised in the hymn of Sundarar and is counted the third of the Nadu Nadu shrines sung in the Tevaram, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The lord is worshipped as Narthanavallabeswarar, the master of the dance, and also as Nerikkattunayakar, a name that can be read as the Lord who shows the way. The goddess is honoured as Gnana Shakti and Para Shakti, and the temple has two shrines to the Mother. The founding patrons of the structural temple are not firmly recorded in the sources consulted.
sections.architecture: The sources say little of the towers and halls of Koodalaiyathur, so this account keeps to what is recorded. The temple is a Shaiva shrine with a sanctum for Narthanavallabeswarar and, unusually, two shrines for the goddess, Gnana Shakti and Para Shakti. Its sacred waters are as much a part of its architecture as its stone: the temple is associated with the Brahma, Agastya and Katyayana theerthas, and it stands beside the river confluence from which the village takes its name.
sections.legends: Two traditions are told of Koodalaiyathur. In the first, Brahma, the creator, longed to witness the dance of Shiva and prayed here with devotion, and the Lord danced before him, which is why he is revered as Narthanavallabeswarar. In the second, the sage Agastya prayed to Shiva for a daughter and found a child floating on a lotus leaf in the waters of the Manimutharu river. The first legend gives the temple its name; the second ties it to the sacred river at its side. The sources consulted do not record a separate legend for the name Nerikkattunayakar.
sections.festivals: The great festival of the temple is the thirteen-day Brahmotsavam of the Tamil month of Masi, kept around Masi Magam in February or March and celebrated with great devotion. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Koodalaiyathur is a place for those who love river and temple together. Walk first to the water where the Vellaru and Manimutharu meet, and then come to the sanctum of Narthanavallabeswarar, the Lord of the dance, and to the two shrines of the Mother. Pilgrims remember Sundarar's hymn and the old tradition that makes this confluence a southern Prayag. The village is quiet and rural, and the temple keeps the calm of a place far from the main roads.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Koodalaiyathur is a village in Kattumannarkoil taluk of Cuddalore district (post office Kavalakudi, PIN 608702), at the confluence of the Vellaru and Manimutharu. By road it is about 31 km south-east of Virudhachalam, reached through Rajendrapattinam and Srimushnam, and it can also be approached from Chidambaram through Kavalakudi. Local buses are infrequent, so plan the last stretch by road and confirm transport on the day.
